comments.textRawHtml: This has the delightful and surely unintentional side effect of all but ensuring all federal agencies who want to use LLMs have to direct their budget to one of the domestic frontier labs (OpenAI, xAI), so that’s a nice big fat pipe of taxpayer money that’ll be going to backstop those cats while they deal with the fact that they’re getting their lunch eaten by competitors who didn’t decide the way to build a sustainable future was to incur future debts to the tune of a sizable percent of the GDP of a G20 nation.

children.author: yipinwong
children.textRawHtml:
You gotta make trade-offs.

Two facets here. Economy and Security. Is current US governemnt in favor of providing cheaper, less SOTA models to Americans at the cost of exposing US content to Chinese firms? Chinese firms by Chinese law are forced to handover whenever CCP asks them to.

Given all sensitive information, the security outjustify the cost here.

There are other areas we need to look at but for my analogy, this should work.

children.author: pms
children.textRawHtml:
Isn't this a misuse of the word steelman, because it wasn't accompanied by the criticism?

From Google Search overview box:

> To steelman means to build the strongest, most charitable version of an opposing argument—even better than the way your opponent stated it—before you criticize or reply to it. It is the exact opposite of a strawman, which is when you intentionally weaken or misrepresent someone's view to make it easy to knock down.

children.author: roughly
children.textRawHtml:
The United States government needs to make tradeoffs. They are as you list.

The Chinese government also needs to make tradeoffs. You can imagine what they are.

You as an individual also need to make tradeoffs. In doing so, you ought be sure to remember you’re not a nation state, you’re an individual human being.

(You may decide “I find myself one small being in a world full of nation states, and given that, I trust the US government to keep me safe, and therefore will align myself with its interests,” at which point “ban DeepSeek” is in your interests as well as those of the US government, but you shouldn’t get the two confused, lest you miss the moments those interests diverge.)

children.author: lopsotronic
children.textRawHtml:
A theoretical scenario: I am a company in the united states making missile seekers.

My software guys say, hey, the imaging infrared seeker is like a zillion percent harder to fool if it has this tiny LLM brain that we blow into the chip. They grab the most optimized model, which so happens to come from a PRC lab. Sure, it's running on all US hardware but, deep down in its little LLM brain, it so happens to be virtually blind to any IR signature that has a pulsed frequency of XXX.

Now all my missiles have what is basically an externally controlled IFF in their little missile brains. "Chinese jet? I see no Chinese jet."

Or what if the pulse contained more instructions? Like, say, "Do a U-Turn and Lock On The Closest Jet Motor You See". A couple of PLAAF pilots watching USN aviators frantically trying to dodge their own missiles - what might possibly be the most embarrassing air-to-air engagement in aviation history.

These models are called nondeterministic for a reason, and it's because the massively complex interrelated weights are incredibly hard to pick apart and audit. It's not like OSS code from a deterministic software program, like a pypi dependency. Now, it's not impossible, and THAT is where the weight of regulation and such SHOULD be going, but, hey, not sure you noticed, US Leadership is not exactly sitting in a surfeit of technical expertise at the moment.

I don't think it's the right call, to blanket ban them, but it's understandable.
